metadata.description:
This artifact is a reproduction package for the STTT article “Bridging Hardware and Software Analysis with Btor2C: A Word-Level-Circuit-to-C Translator (Extended Version).”

It consists of source code, precompiled binaries, and input data used in the evaluation of the paper, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the source code of the translator Btor2C, the benchmark suite and the executables of the hardware/software analyzers used in the evaluation, the raw data generated from the evaluation, scripts to run the experiments, and instructions for reproducing the tables and figures in the paper.

metadata.title: Reproduction Package for ASE 2025 Paper "Non-termination Witnesses and Their Validation"
metadata.description:
Reproduction Package for the Paper “Non-termination Witnesses and Their Validation”

Abstract

This artifact is a reproduction package for the paper “Non-termination Witnesses and Their Validation” which has been accepted at ASE 2025.

It consists of all executables, input data and results required to reproduce the experiments. In particular, it also contains the original results of the paper and a way to generate the macros and csv’s to generate the plots in the paper from it.

We run the experiments using 2 cores and 15 GiB of memory for at most 15 minutes (CPU time).

A full reproduction of the experiments requires roughly 40 days of CPU time. For demonstration purposes, a subset of tasks has been selected which should take at most 1 day to complete and will likely finish sooner. To test that everything is working as intended, we provide a configuration that terminates within ~10 minutes.

Contents

This artifact contains the following items:

  • README.md: This file.
  • benchmark-defs/*.xml.template: Templates to generate benchmark definition files for running the experiments using BenchExec.
  • benchmark-defs/set_tasks.py: Script to change the tasks to be run in the xml files.
  • tasks/*.xml: Sets of tasks
    • tasks/all.xml: All tasks used to produce the results in the paper.
    • tasks/subset.xml: Subset of the tasks used in the paper.
    • test/test.xml: One task used only for the smoke test of the Artifact.
  • data-analysis: Scripts and definitions to produce the CSV files used to generate the plots in the paper. Additionally they also generate the macros used to generate the tables in the paper.
  • benchmark-utils/*: Benchmarking utils
    • config.sh: File with parameters for BenchExec
    • check_configured.sh: File which checks that BenchExec is set up correctly
  • Makefile: Makefile to run the experiments.
  • results-paper: Raw results of the experiments presented in the paper.
  • License.txt: License information for the artifact.
  • sv-benchmarks: The SV-COMP25 benchmarks. Unnecessary files have been removed to make the artifact smaller.
  • Tools can be found in the tools directory.
    • CPAchecker: CPAchecker version b20e3a16.
    • UAuomizer: UAutomizer in its SV-COMP25 version in the folder uautomizer.
    • TransVer: TransVer at commit fd9c9ac6 in the folder transver using CPAchecker at commit 66247485
    • Symbiotic: Symbiotic at commit 9cd025a built for Ubuntu in the folder symbiotic
    • EmergenTheta: EmergenTheta at commit 3caaa21 in the folder emergentheta
    • Theta: Theta at commit 3caaa21 in the folder theta
    • Theta: Theta at commit 3caaa21 in the folder theta-modular
    • Thorn: Theta at commit 3caaa21 in the folder thorn
    • witch: Witch at commit b717fec built for Ubuntu in the folder witch
    • WitnessLint: WitnessLint at commit 5dabcf0f in the folder witnesslint

This README contains the following sections to help the user to reproduce the experiments:

  • TL;DR: A quick guide to reproduce the experiments and analyze the data.
  • Environment: Describes the environment in which the artifact was tested and can be run.
  • Experiments: Describes how to execute the experiments and generate the results.
  • Results: Describes where the results can be found and how to analyze them.
  • Known Issues: Describes known issues when executing the artifact.
  • Reuse: Documentation on how to reuse the artifact for other purposes.

TL;DR

  1. Extract the files in the provided ZIP archive to an arbitrary directory and open a terminal inside it.
  2. Set the environment variables:
  • source benchmark-utils/local_config.sh: if you have a overlayfs in version 1.10 or newer installed
  1. Choose one of the following sets of tasks to run:
    • make setup-benchmark: Reproduce all results in our paper on your machine (takes about 30 days of CPU time, requires 2 cores and 16GiB of RAM). We strongly discourage from running this inside a VM.
    • make setup-subset: Reproduce the results on a representative subset of our tasks (takes ~1 day).
    • make setup-test: Smoke test the VM and the setup (takes ~5 min).
  2. Run make transform-programs-termination to transform the programs to be used for non-termination analysis.
  3. Run make verify-all to run the verification of all the tools to export the witnesses.
  4. Run make process-all-witnesses to generate the directories from which the witnesses will be read from. This symlinks the witnesses into that directory.
  5. Run make validate-all to validate all the produced witnesses by all the verifiers.
  6. Run make process-results to process the produced results in order to get human readable results. They can be found in the results/tables directory. The tex macros with p-values from Wilcoxon test are generated in results/wilcoxon-p-values.tex.

Environment

To run the artifact BenchExec, Python >= 3.8, and Java >= 21 are required. We attach Symbiotic and Witch as builds for Ubuntu. We use Ubuntu 24.04 LTS as the base system to test the artifact. Furthermore, we recommend using a VM with at least 16 GiB of RAM and 4 cores to run the experiments.

Inside a clean VM, please see the documentation of the respective tools for installation hints. A non-exhaustive list of required packages:

  • CPAchecker: Java 17
  • UAutomizer: Java 21 
  • Symbiotic and Witch: LLVM 14 and python3-clang-14
  • Theta, EmergenTheta, Thorn, Theta-modular: Java 17, libgomp1, libmpfr6

NOTE: We assume that all of the following commands are executed from inside the root directory of the artifact!

Experiments

Setup

Run source benchmark-utils/local_config.sh (needs to be repeated every time a new shell is opened).

Benchmark Selection

Depending on your available resources you can select different sets of benchmarks to execute the tools on. You have the following options:

  • A quick test with a single file, which can be useful to test that the artifact is behaving as intended. To select it use make setup-test. Executing this benchmark set should take ~5 minutes.
  • A subset of the tasks used for the benchmarks in the paper. To select it use make setup-subset. Executing this benchmark set should take around 1 day.
  • The full benchmark set used in the experiments. To select it use make setup-benchmark. Executing this benchmark set will take around 30 days of CPU Time.

Running the Experiments

To run all experiments multiple targets need to be executed one after the other, their list and order can be found in the TL;DR. Each of them encompass multiple targets for the different verifiers and validator backends.

All experiments are run using BenchExec in order to ensure reliable benchmarks.

Results

Generating the Results

Once you ran all experiments execute make process-results to generate HTML tables which contain the information used in RQ1 and RQ2. The tex macros with p-values from Wilcoxon test are generated in results/wilcoxon-p-values.tex.

To analyze the results of RQ3 please take a look at this README

Known Issues

Warnings

Overheating

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the CPU was throttled due to overheating. This affects the time measurements in the results, but should not happen when reproducing the results outside a VM.

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - CPU throttled itself during benchmarking due to overheating. Benchmark results are unreliable!

Overlayfs

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the home directory should be given as an overlay or hidden. Currently it is not possible to do neither of those inside the TACAS23 VM due to its old overlayfs and due to not knowing the path to the folder where the artifact is being executed.

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - Home directory in container should be /home/benchexec but this directory cannot be created due to directory mode of parent directory. It is recommended to use '--overlay-dir /home' or '--hidden-dir /home' and overwrite directory modes for subdirectories where necessary.

Resource Requirements

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the resource requirements are being ignored. This only means that the resource requirements regarding CPU model are being ignored, this has no effect on the benchmarking.

Errors

Overlay

When BenchExec tries to create an overlay mount while there is a shared folder mounted inside the VM, the following error may occur:

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - ERROR - Failed to create overlay mount for /home/...: invalid argument ...

In this case, the shared folder should be unmounted and the experiments should be run again.

C Groups

If BenchExec is unable to use C groups to benchmark then a restart of the VM may help make BenchExec work as intended.

Z3 not working properly

This artifact includes the tools from SVCOMP25 built for the setup of that competition. On other systems, this may cause errors if the CPU instruction set differs. In particular, Virtual Box does not support the avx instruction set on Windows hosts with Hyper-V active. This can cause Ultimate Automizer to fail. To circumvent this, try evaluating the artifact on a different host system, try disabling Hyper-V in Windows (see e.g. https://forums.virtualbox.org/viewtopic.php?f=25&t=99390) or rebuild the affected tools.

For the last option run the following commands:

sudo apt -y install z3
mv ./tools/uautomizer/z3 ./tools/uautomizer/z3_original
sudo ln /usr/bin/z3 ./tools/uautomizer/z3

Wilcoxon p-value calculation

When calculating the p-values for the Wilcoxon test, it may happen that an error occurs due to there being too few data points. This can for example happen when using the test benchmark set.

Reuse

For developing and reusing this artifact for other purposes please look at developing.md.

metadata.title: Reproduction Package for STTT 2025 Article `TransVer: A Modular Program-Transformation Framework for Reduction to Reachability'
metadata.description:
TransVer: A Modular Program-Transformation Framework for Reduction to Reachability

Abstract

This is the Artifact for the paper “TransVer: A Modular Program-Transformation Framework for Reduction to Reachability” which has been submitted to journal STTT in 2025.

The STTT article presents a program transformation framework with the goal of verifying different properties with of-the-shelf reachability analyzers. The transformations are in a framework based on instrumentation automata, inspired by the BLAST query language. In our initial study, we support four important concrete specifications for C programs: termination, no-overflow, memory cleanup, and memory safety. This artifact can be used to reproduce the experiments presented in the paper. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our transformations by comparing verifiers that support the specifications natively with verifiers for reachability applied to the transformed programs. The results are very promising: Our transformations can extend existing verifiers to be effective on specifications that they do not support natively, and that the efficiency is often similar to verifiers that natively support the considered specifications.

The artifact consists of Makefile that can be used to setup all the tools and environment for the experiments. Moreover, it provides a simple interface for running all the scripts. Furthermore, it contains benchmarking definitions used by BenchExec to execute the experiments and processing scripts of the results that were used to generate the tables. The folder figures-generation/results-STTT2025-submission/ contains all the data that we computed.

We assign 4 CPU cores, 15 GB of memory, and 900s of CPU time limit to each verification task. A reproduction of the full experiments would require more than 2 months of CPU time. Therefore, we prepared a subset of benchmarks for which the reproduction is faster. This reproduction package is intended to be run on the TACAS VM or on an Ubuntu 24.04 machine. Otherwise, the installation of the provided packages can break the operation system. If you wish to run it on a different OS, please install the requirements separately. We recommend viewing this README in its .html form as some links might not work otherwise.

Contents

  • README.md: this file containing documentation and useful tips
  • benchmark-defs/: directory with the requirement definitions for each tool required by BenchExec
  • benchmark-utils/: directory with scripts that check for the environment requirements for BenchExec
    • benchmark-utils/config.sh: file with parameters for BenchExec
    • benchmark-utils/check_configured.sh: file which checks that BenchExec is set up correctly
  • complete_logs/*: directory with logs from benchexec for all the tools and properties for smoke tests
  • figures-generation/: directory with scripts and definitions to produce the CSV files used to generate the plots in the paper
    • figures-generation/results-STTT2025-submission: raw results of the experiments presented in the paper
    • figures-generation/results-STTT2025-submission/final-table.html: all the results merged into an interactive table with CPU time, memory consumption and verdicts
  • scripts/ directory with scripts used to process the benchmarks
  • tasks/: directory with sets of tasks
    • tasks/{property}/all.xml: all tasks used to produce the results in the paper
    • tasks/{property}/subset.xml: subset of the tasks used in the paper
    • test/{property}/test.xml: one task used only for the smoke test of the artifact
  • transver/: directory of our tool TransVer that transforms the programs
  • Makefile: makefile with all the commands to set-up the environments, transform and verify all or just a subset of programs
  • License.txt: license information for the artifact
  • sv-benchmarks.zip: the SV-COMP25 benchmarks
  • packages: archive containing all the required packages
  • Tools:
    • Aprove: in archive aprove.zip
    • Bubaak: in archive bubaak.zip
    • CPAchecker: in archive cpachecker.zip
    • UAutomizer: in archive uautomizer.zip
    • UTaipan: in archive utaipan.zip
    • UKojak: in archive ukojak.zip
    • Symbiotic: in archive symbiotic.zip
    • CPV: in archive cpv.zip
    • Theta: in archive Theta.zip
    • EmergenTheta: in archive EmergenTheta.zip
    • TransVer: TransVer at commit 1a9ea890 in the folder transver using CPAchecker at commit 6143fde0

This README guides an user through the following steps:

  • A Modular Program-Transformation Framework for Reducing Specifications to Reachability
    • Abstract
    • Contents
    • TL;DR
    • Smoke Tests
    • Reusability
    • Set up the Environment
    • Experiments
    • Trouble Shooting

To reproduce the claims for our research questions, one needs to run the following:

  • RQ1: Verifiers can succesfully verify properties they do not natively support.
    • (a) Termination: One needs to transform the tasks with the termination transformation and run:
      • CPV, Theta, EmergenTheta on the transformed tasks
      • Aprove on the respective original tasks
    • (b) No-overflow: One needs to transform the tasks with the no-overflow transformation and run:
      • CPV, Theta, EmergenTheta on the transformed tasks
      • UKojak on the respective original tasks
  • RQ2 & RQ3: State-of-the-art reachability verifiers can be as effective and efficient as the native verifiers.
    • (a) Termination: One needs to transform the tasks with the termination transformation and run:
      • CPAchecker, UAutomizer on the transformed tasks
      • Aprove, UAutomizer on the respective original tasks
    • (b) No-overflow: One needs to transform the tasks with the no-overflow transformation and run:
      • CPAchecker, UAutomizer on the transformed tasks
      • UKojak, UAutomizer, UTaipan on the respective original tasks
    • (c) Memory-cleanup: One needs to transform the tasks with the memory-cleanup transformation and run:
      • CPAchecker, UAutomizer on the transformed tasks
      • Symbiotic, Bubaak, CPAchecker on the respective original tasks
    • (d) Memory-safety: One needs to transform the tasks with the memory-safety transformation and run:
      • CPAchecker, UAutomizer on the transformed tasks
      • Symbiotic, UAutomizer, CPAchecker on the respective original tasks
  • RQ4: Reducing the verification task on C programs is not less efficient than doing the reduction on an intermediate abstraction.
    • (a) No-overflow: One needs to transform the tasks with the no-overflow transformation and run:
      • CPAchecker with predicate abstraction on the transformed tasks
      • CPAchecker on the respective original tasks
    • (b) Termination: One needs to transform the tasks with the termination transformation and run:
      • CPAchecker with termination-to-safety analysis on the transformed tasks
      • CPAchecker on the respective original tasks

TL;DR

  1. The full experiment runs require at least 15 GB of available memory and at least 4 available CPUs. If you run the artifact on TACAS VM, you can specify how much memory and how many CPUs you wish to allow to use:
vboxmanage import TACAS23-AEC.ova --vsys 0 --memory 16384 --cpus 4

If you do not have 16 GB of memory available, you can lower the limits for the runs to 7 GB with make set-lower-memory-limits. WARNING: After lowering the memory, our results will probably not be fully reproduced. (to switch back to 15GB, one can run make set-bigger-memory-limits)

  1. If inside the TACAS23 VM: If you use shared folder to load the artifact directory into the VM, please create a copy of the artifact on the VM and run all the commands from there cp -r <path_to_shared_folder>/<artifact_directory> /home/tacas23/. All the remaining steps should be then run from /home/tacas23/<artifact_directory>. The reason is that it might happen that the VM does not have permission to write or move files inside the shared folder.

  2. Setup variables in your shell environment(WARNING: this needs to be executed again after closing a terminal):

    • To execute on your local system or virtual machine use source benchmark-utils/config.sh.
    • If you have access to a BenchCloud instance use source benchmark-utils/config_vcloud.sh, adapting it correspondingly to your server.

  3. If inside the TACAS23 VM: Run make install-packages to install all needed packages, which are available with their corresponding license under packages.

    • WARNING: these packages are meant to be installed on the TACAS virtual machine or on a machine with Ubuntu 22.04 ! Installing them on a machine with different operating system might cause problems. Please refer to Trouble Shooting section for encountered errors.

  4. Run make setup-all to unzip all the needed tools and benchmarks. This step may take some time

  5. Select the tasks which you would like to use:

    • make setup-test: to setup a few tasks to test the functionality of the artifact
    • make setup-subset: to setup tasks to run a representative subset of tasks for the experiments in the paper
    • make setup-benchmark: to setup all tasks used in the experiments in the paper

  6. Transform the properties to reachability using make transform-programs. The transformed programs can be found in transformed_tasks_*/ and the original programs in original_tasks_*/.

  7. Execute the verification tasks on the original properties using make experiments-original-property

    • This command will run BenchExec to measure the resources consumed during the verification process. It is possible that after running it for the first time, one needs to create a partition in cgroups for BenchExec manually. If there is an error when running it for the first time, please run make add-cgroup-partition, for more details, we refer a reader to Trouble Shooting section of this file.
    • Executing the verification of all the tools for all the properties may take up to 1 hour. If you wish to run the tools for different properties, please have a look at Smoke Test.

  8. Execute the verification tasks where the original property has been encoded as a reachability property using make experiments-transformed

    • Executing the verification of all the tools for all the properties may take up to 1 hour. If you wish to run the tools for different properties, please have a look at Smoke Test.

Set up the Environment

To run the artifact BenchExec, Python >= 3.8, Java 17 and Podman are required. We provide an archive packages.zip with all required packages and the corresponding licenses. Follow the steps to install all of them either on your machine or on provided TACAS VM. If you run the artifact on TACAS VM, please allocate at least 15 GB of memory and 4 CPUs. This can be done with loading the VM with the following command:

vboxmanage import TACAS23-AEC.ova --vsys 0 --memory 16384 --cpus 4

NOTE: We assume that all of the commands are executed from inside the root directory of the artifact!

  1. If inside the TACAS23 VM: If you use shared folder to load the artifact directory into the VM, please create a copy of the artifact on the VM and run all the commands from there cp -r <path_to_shared_folder>/<artifact_directory> /home/tacas23/. All the remaining steps should be then run from /home/tacas23/<artifact_directory>. The reason is that it might happen that the VM does not have permission to write or move files inside the shared folder.
  2. run source benchmark-utils/config.sh (WARNING: needs to be repeated every time a new shell is opened)
  3. make setup-all to unzip all the archives with the tools and benchmarks
  4. If inside the TACAS23 VM: make install-packages to install all the required packages
  5. make switch-cgroup to switch to cgroups V1 which are needed to run benchexec
  6. If you do not have 15 GB of memory available, you can lower the limits for the runs to 7 GB with make set-lower-memory-limits. WARNING: After lowering the memory, our results will probably not be fully reproduced. (to switch back to 15GB, one can run make set-bigger-memory-limits)

Smoke Tests

Running our full experiments requires around 2 months of CPU time. We have selected few testing programs for quicker evaluation. The goal is to demonstrate the overall procedure that we did in order to run the experiments for our research questions. In this section, we explain how to run each transformation for handful of programs and how to verify them with each of the used tools. We assume that all the packages are installed, and that the tools and benchmarks are unzipped, following the Set up section.

Termination

We have chosen the following programs to demonstrate the termination transformation:

  • sv-benchmarks/c/termination-crafted/2Nested-1.c (expected verdict true)
  • sv-benchmarks/c/termination-crafted/Bangalore_v2.c (expected verdict false)
  1. run make setup-test-termination to prepare set files with these two programs
  2. run make transform-programs-termination to transform these two programs, their transformed versions are stored in transformed_tasks_t2r/ and their original versions are copied to original_tasks_t2r/
  3. The following commands will execute BenchExec to measure the performance of the verification tools, if you run it for the first time, it is possible, that it will throw an error. If that is the case, please run make add-cgroup-partition and this error should be fixed until switching off the machine. WARNING: This should be run after running at least once benchexec (i.e. some of the make experiment-* commands).
  4. run all the verifiers to test whether they work properly (some of them may take up to 15 minutes, as they are not able to solve the tasks in time), moreover some of them throw a known error on them which is expected:

    • make experiment-aprove-verification-termination
  • tools verifying reachability:
    • make experiment-uautomizer-verification-termination-transformed (Expected outcome: complete_logs/uautomizer_termination_transformed.txt)
    • make experiment-cpachecker-verification-termination-transformed (Expected outcome: complete_logs/cpachecker_termination_transformed.txt)
    • make experiment-cpv-verification-termination-transformed (Expected outcome: complete_logs/cpv_termination_transformed.txt)
    • make experiment-theta-verification-termination-transformed (Expected outcome: complete_logs/theta_termination_transformed.txt)

In this section, we discuss the known problems and possible ways how to solve them when running this artifact.

Cgroups for BenchExec

It is possible that when running BenchExec for the first time (especially on the TACAS VM), there is the following error:

2025-04-06 12:49:46,968 - WARNING - Ignoring specified resource requirements in local-execution mode, only resource limits are used.
2025-04-06 12:49:47,009 - INFO - Unable to find pqos_wrapper, please install it for cache allocation and monitoring if your CPU supports Intel RDT (cf. https://gitlab.com/sosy-lab/software/pqos-wrapper).
2025-04-06 12:49:47,009 - WARNING - Cgroup subsystem cpuset is not available. Please make sure it is supported by your kernel and available.
2025-04-06 12:49:47,009 - ERROR - Cgroup subsystem cpuset is required for limiting the number of CPU cores/memory nodes.

The kernel has a bug where delegation of cpuset does not work if there are processes of other users in this user's cgroup.
This happens commonly if xdg-document-portal is running while such delegation is attempted for the first time.
For more information cf. https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/18293.
Linux 6.6 is expected to contain a fix for this bug.

As a quick workaround, execute this command, which forces the missing delegation as root user:
  echo +cpuset | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/benchexec.slice/cgroup.subtree_control

To fix this issue, run the following command:

make add-cgroup-partition

WARNING: This command needs to be run after BenchExec was executed at least once. It needs to be run only once and then it works until the restart of the machine.

Expected Errors when Installing the Packages

The installation command make install-packages might throw some errors for already installed packages or for packages that are not needed in the reproduction of the experiments. However, these errors do not influence the reproduction of our experiments and can be ignored. Specifically for the TACAS VM, we expect the following errors:

 packages/python3_3.10.6-1~22.04.1_amd64.deb
make: *** [Makefile:98: install-packages] Error 1

Failed Instrumentation

When running make transform-programs-{property}, there might be a warning for some of the programs that looks like this:

The instrumentation of file {file} failed !

Please, ignore this warning. This just means that the program contains unsupported features for our transformation framework (like arrays for termination transformation) and therefore, TransVer does not transform the program.

CPU-throttling warnings

When you are running experiments (especially on a laptop), BenchExec might raise the following warning:

2024-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - CPU throttled itself during benchmarking due to overheating. Benchmark results are unreliable!

This is normal on a laptop. Please ignore it.

metadata.title: Reproduction Package for CAV 2025 Article `Btor2-Select: Machine Learning Based Algorithm Selection for Hardware Model Checking'
metadata.description:
Abstract

This artifact is a reproduction package for the article “Btor2-Select: Machine Learning Based Algorithm Selection for Hardware Model Checking”, published at CAV 2025. The artifact has been evaluated and awarded the badges of Available, Functional, and Reusable. It is archived on Zenodo with the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15485472.

The paper investigates machine-learning-based algorithm selection for hardware model checking in the Btor2 language. It proposes a framework to train an algorithm selector that predicts the best available off-the-shelf model checker for a given verification task. The selector then invokes the predicted backend model checker to solve the task.

This artifact supports the reproduction of:

  1. the training of the algorithm selector using the provided performance data and
  2. the evaluation of the algorithm selector (integrated with backend model checkers) against state-of-the-art hardware model checkers.

The artifact consists of source code, precompiled executables, and input data used in the training and evaluation of the paper, as well as the results produced from the experiments. Specifically, it includes the selector trained by our framework, the backend verifiers to be selected, a set of Btor2 verification tasks collected for training and evaluation, the experimental data generated from the evaluation, and instructions to run the tools and experiments.

Artifact Requirements

This reproduction package works best with the SoSy-Lab Virtual Machine, which runs Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and has all the required dependencies installed. If you test the artifact with this VM, you do not need to install any package. Please login the VM as user vagrant via GUI or SSH. The VM has been tested with VirtualBox 7.0 on a Linux (Ubuntu 24.04) computer.

The benchmarking framework BenchExec used in our experiments relies on control groups and namespaces provided by modern Linux kernels. Our tool, Btor2-Select, was tested with Python 3.12. Additionally, one of the compared tools, super_prove, is executed in a containerized environment with Podman (tested with version 4.9.3).

To perform most of the experiments included in this artifact, a machine with 16 GB of RAM, 4 CPU cores, and 15 GB of disk space is needed.

A full reproduction of the training part required around 8.5 hours of wall-clock time on a server equipped with 2 TB of RAM and two 2.0 GHz AMD EPYC 7713 CPUs, each with 128 processing units. The evaluation phase consumed more than 776 hours of CPU time on machines with 3.4 GHz processors. For demonstration purposes, a subset of benchmark tasks can be used. Training on a subset of 450 Btor2 tasks took approximately less than a minute, while evaluation on 30 selected simple Btor2 tasks took roughly 5 minutes on a standard laptop. This artifact README includes time estimates for the various commands referenced throughout.

The uncompressed package takes around 14 GB of disk space. Please make sure there is enough disk space available before extracting it. If you only want to run experiments on the bit-vector tasks, you can exclude the directory perf-eval-hwmc/benchmarks/array when unzipping the package.

Contents

This artifact contains the following items:

  • README.{html,md}: this documentation (we recommend viewing the HTML version with a browser)
  • LICENSE.txt: license information of the artifact
  • btor2-select/: the machine-learning-based framework for algorithm selection and the trained selector (our open-source project, at commit b6505455)
    • bin/: contains the executables of Btor2-Select and Btor2-Para (a parallel portfolio constructed for evaluating Btor2-Select)
    • btor2select/: contains the main production codes for Btor2-Select, including:
      • btor2_select.py: performs inference using the trained selector and executes the selected backend model checker
      • train.py: trains the proposed algorithm selector
      • cross_validation.py: conducts cross-validation analysis
      • Other supporting scripts for different ML models, e.g., PWC-SVM-BoKW, PWC-SVM-WL
    • data/demo/: a small collection of Btor2 verification tasks and their performance data, intended for use in a training demo.
    • README: for additional information
  • perf-eval-hwmc: a directory for evaluating performance of backend model checkers, consisting of:
    • benchmarks/: a set of Btor2 verification tasks collected for training and evaluation
    • dataset/: the performance dataset used for training
    • verifiers/: tool archives of several backend model checkers (including both hardware and software verifiers)
    • benchexec/: a checkout of BenchExec, a reliable benchmarking framework with precise resource management, used to perform the evaluation
    • bench-defs/: benchmark definitions used by BenchExec
    • README: for further information
  • data-submission/: a directory containing the raw and processed data obtained from our experiments
    • cross_val/: the cross-validation results
    • evaluation/: the evaluation results of Btor2-Select, Btor2-Para, ABC, AVR, rIC3, and super_prove
      • paper-results/: the results presented in the paper
      • demo-results/: the results of the demo runs
  • Makefile: a file that assembles commands for running experiments and processing data

Reproduction Package for the Paper “Synthesis of Precise Error Conditions”

Abstract

This artifact is a reproduction package for the paper “Synthesis of Precise Error Conditions” which has been submitted to ASE 2025.

It consists of all executables, input data and results required to reproduce the experiments. In particular it also contains the original results of the paper and a way to generate the plots in the paper from it.

We run the experiments using 8 cores and 31 GB of memory for at most 200 minutes (CPU time). In the artifact we reduce the limits to 4 cores and 8GB of memory. While the reduction of cores will only affect the results related to the Wall Time (RQ2, RQ3, RQ4), the reduced memory limit might lead to more out-of-memory exceptions in this artifact affecting all results.

A full reproduction of the experiments requires roughly 2 years of CPU time. For demonstration purposes, a subset of tasks has been selected which should take at most 1 day to complete and will likely finish sooner. To test that everything is working as intended, we provide a configuration that terminates within ~5 minutes.

The reproduction package can be found in Zenodo.

Contents

This artifact contains the following items:

  • README.md: This file.
  • benchmark-defs/*.xml.template: Templates to generate benchmark definition files for running the experiments using BenchExec.
  • benchmark-defs/set_tasks.py: Script to change the tasks to be run in the xml files.
  • benchmark-defs/tasks*.txt: Sets of tasks
    • benchmark-defs/tasks-all.txt: All tasks used to produce the results in the paper.
    • benchmark-defs/tasks-subset.txt: Subset of the tasks used in the paper.
    • benchmark-defs/tasks-one.txt: Two tasks used only for the smoke test of the Artifact.
  • data-analysis: Scripts and definitions to produce the CSV files used to generate the plots in the paper.
  • config.sh: Configs with parameters for BenchExec.
  • Makefile: Makefile to run the experiments.
  • results-paper: Raw results of the experiments presented in the paper.
  • License.txt: License information for the artifact.
  • sv-benchmarks: The SV-COMP25 benchmarks, without tasks and programs which were not used in the experiments in order to make the artifact smaller.
  • 2025-05-31_submission_ASE25.pdf: The paper as submitted to ASE25.
  • Tools
    • CPAchecker: CPAchecker version Removed for Anonimity in the folder cpachecker.
    • DescribErr: DescribErr version Removed for Anonimity
    • BenchExec: BenchExec version 3.29 in the folder benchexec.

This ReadMe contains the following sections to help the user to reproduce the experiments:

  • TL;DR: A quick guide to reproduce the experiments and analyze the data.
  • Environment: Describes the environment in which the artifact was tested and can be run.
  • Example from the paper: A short description on how to execute example presented in the paper
  • Experiments: Describes how to execute the experiments and generate the results.
  • Results: Describes where the results can be found and how to analyze them.
  • Known Issues: Describes known issues when executing the artifact.

IMPORTANT: Terms Soundness and Completeness in DescribErr

DescribErr internally uses the words overapproximating and underapproximating for sound and complete, respectively.

TL;DR

We tested the artifact inside the TACAS23 VM (Ubuntu 22.04) with username and password being tacas23. To run DescribErr on single examples, 4 cores and 8GB of RAM are sufficient (cf. Section ‘Example from the paper’).

  1. Extract the files in the provided ZIP archive to an arbitrary directory and open a terminal inside it.
  2. Setup the environment of the VM using ./setup_vm.sh (requires root and will reboot your system).
  3. Set the environment variables:
  • source config_clean_vm.sh: if full read/write access for all tools to /home is fine (recommended in the TACAS VM)
  • source config.sh: if you have a overlayfs in version 1.10 or newer installed
  1. Optional: Run DescribErr on the motivating example on the paper with make paper-example
  2. Choose one of the following sets of tasks to run
    • make setup-benchmark: Reproduce all results in our paper on your machine (takes about 2 years of CPU time, requires 8 cores and 31GB of RAM). We strongly discourage from running this inside the VM.
    • make setup-benchmark-vm: Reproduce all results in our paper on your machine (takes about 2 years of CPU time, requires 4 cores and 8GB of RAM; final results might differ because of reduced resources).
    • make setup-subset: Reproduce the results on a representative subset of our tasks (takes ~1 day and requires only 8 GB of RAM).
    • make setup-testing: Smoke test the VM and the setup (takes ~5 min and requires only 8 GB of RAM).
  3. Run make experiments to run the experiments for CPAchecker and DescribErr. If you do not want to re-run the experiments in the paper, but continue the pipeline using our results execute cp -r results-paper results.
  4. Run make process-results to generate the results as HTML tables, raw CSV and plots used in the paper. Find them here: results/output.

Environment

The easiest way to use this artifact is using the TACAS23 VM, copying the contents of the artifact to the VM, and setting it up by using ./setup_vm.sh inside the root directory of the artifact (i.e., setup_vm.sh is visible). This should work for any clean Ubuntu VM.

To run the artifact BenchExec, Python >= 3.8, and Java >= 17 are required. Additionally the python packages matplotlib==3.10.3, scipy==1.15.3, pandas==2.2.3, venny4py==1.0.3, pyyaml==6.0.2, and seaborn==0.13.2 are required to generate the plots. Script setup_vm.sh takes care of their installation. A restart of the system is required.

Inside a clean VM, please see the documentation of the respective tools for installation hints. A non-exhaustive list of required packages: * CPAchecker: Java 17 * DescribErr: Python 3.10

NOTE: We assume that all of the following commands are executed from inside the root directory of the artifact!

Example from the paper

The motivating example of the paper can be found under: describerr/examples/primefactors-example.c

To find the precise error condition x % -4 == 0 || (-128 < x && x <= 0) for it you can use the custom configuration ./describerr/examples/primefactors-config.yml. In the interest of time, we restrict the config to only consider == as relation operator and % as arithmetic operator. We also showcase the extensibility of DescribErr by running a parallel portfolio of the verifiers CPAchecker and CBMC as validator for this example. The following command line shows how to execute the motivating example from the shell:

./describerr/describ-err.py --program describerr/examples/primefactors-example.c ./describerr/examples/primefactors-config.yml

Please be aware that this may take up to 45 minutes.

DescribErr uses the word overapproximating in the logs if it was able to prove an error condition to be sound. Analogously, it uses the word underapproximating in the logs if it was able to prove an error condition to be complete.

Experiments

Setup

Run source config.sh (needs to be repeated every time a new shell is opened).

Benchmark Selection

Depending on your available resources you can select different sets of benchmarks to execute the tools on. You have the following options:

  • A quick test with two files, which can be useful to test that the artifact is behaving as intended. To select it use make setup-testing. Executing this benchmark set should take ~5 minutes.
  • A subset of the tasks used for the benchmarks in the paper. To select it use make setup-subset. Executing this benchmark set should take around 1 day.
  • The full benchmark set used in the experiments. To select it use make setup-benchmark to run it with the original resource limits of 31GB RAM and 8 cores (or make setup-benchmark-vm to run it with 4 cores and 8GB of RAM). Executing this benchmark set will take around 2 years of CPU Time.

Running the Experiments

To run all experiments sequentially execute make experiments. This is a make target encompassing the following experiments, each represented as a make target:

  • experiment-cpachecker-verification-svcomp25: Executes CPAchecker on the benchmarks selected using predicate analysis. This is the same analysis which DescribErr uses internally for validating the error conditions in our experiments.
  • experiment-describerr-template: Executes the template analysis of DescribErr.
  • experiment-describerr-template-daikon: Executes the template analysis of DescribErr boosted with the error condition candidates generated by DAIKON.
  • experiment-describerr-interval: Executes the interval analysis of DescribErr.
  • experiment-describerr-interval-daikon: Executes the interval analysis of DescribErr boosted with error condition candidates generated by DAIKON which are in the form of an interval.
  • experiment-describerr-counterexample: Executes the counterexample analysis of DescribErr.

All experiments are run using BenchExec in order to ensure reliable benchmarks.

Results

Generating the Results

Once you ran all experiments execute make process-results to generate the results as HTML tables, raw CSV and plots used in the paper. You will find them here: results/output.

Known Issues

Warnings

Overheating

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the CPU was throttled due to overheating. This affects the time measurements in the results, but should not happen when reproducing the results outside a VM.

2025-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - CPU throttled itself during benchmarking due to overheating. Benchmark results are unreliable!

Overlayfs

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the home directory should be given as an overlay or hidden. Currently it is not possible to do neither of those inside the TACAS23 VM due to its old overlayfs and due to not knowing the path to the folder where the artifact is being executed.

2025-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - WARNING - Home directory in container should be /home/benchexec but this directory cannot be created due to directory mode of parent directory. It is recommended to use '--overlay-dir /home' or '--hidden-dir /home' and overwrite directory modes for subdirectories where necessary.

Resource Requirements

During the execution of the experiments, a warning may appear which tells us that the resource requirements are being ignored. This only means that the resource requirements regarding CPU model are being ignored, this has no effect on the benchmarking.

Errors

Overlay

When BenchExec tries to create an overlay mount while there is a shared folder mounted inside the VM, the following error may occur:

2025-XX-XX XX:XX:XX - ERROR - Failed to create overlay mount for /home/...: invalid argument ...

In this case, the shared folder should be unmounted and the experiments should be run again.

C Groups

If BenchExec is unable to use C groups to benchmark and you have already run ./setup_vm.sh then a restart of the VM will help make BenchExec work as intended.
